faq.q: Can muscle hypertrophy occur without exercise?

Providing amino acids within 2 h post‑exercise maximises mTOR activation and protein synthesis.

exam: What bedside test would you use to monitor progress in a patient with HIV‑related wasting? — Hand‑grip dynamometry; it reflects functional muscle strength.
A patient on a low‑protein diet starts resistance training but shows no size gain. What is the most likely cause? — Inadequate protein intake; muscle protein synthesis cannot exceed breakdown.
How does mTORC1 integrate nutritional signals to drive hypertrophy? — It senses leucine and insulin/IGF‑1, promoting translation initiation and satellite‑cell activation.
Why is compartment syndrome a contraindication to continued resistance training? — Increased pressure compromises perfusion, risking irreversible muscle necrosis.
In a rural clinic without ultrasound, how would you assess muscle hypertrophy? — Measure mid‑upper arm circumference and compare to baseline; track functional strength.
Explain why anabolic steroids are avoided in low‑resource settings despite their hypertrophic effect. — High cost, liver toxicity, and risk of cardiovascular events outweigh benefits.
A patient with chronic TB shows muscle wasting. Which intervention targets the underlying catabolism? — Effective anti‑TB therapy combined with protein‑rich diet and resistance exercises.
Distinguish true hypertrophy from pseudohypertrophy on physical exam. — True hypertrophy yields increased strength; pseudohypertrophy shows larger girth but weak power.
ai.title: Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Skeletal muscle hypertrophy is the increase in muscle fiber size due to protein synthesis outweighing breakdown. It is driven by mechanical load, metabolic stress, and hormonal signals, and has clinical relevance for rehabilitation, chronic disease, and performance.

b: Two main types: myofibrillar (strength) and sarcoplasmic (size).
Requires adequate nutrition, especially protein and calories.
sections.p: Hypertrophy refers to enlargement of existing muscle fibers, not an increase in fiber number. It occurs when repeated overload stimulates anabolic pathways, leading to net protein accretion.

b: mTORC1 integrates growth factor (IGF‑1) and amino‑acid signals.
Satellite cell activation peaks 24‑48 h after exercise.
sections.p: Mechanical tension, metabolic stress, and muscle damage activate mTORC1, MAPK, and satellite cell proliferation. Satellite cells donate nuclei, supporting larger cytoplasmic volume.

b: Resistance training improves functional status in older adults.
In low‑resource settings, simple body‑weight programs can counteract cachexia.
sections.p: Understanding hypertrophy guides physiotherapy after immobilisation, sarcopenia management, and recovery from chronic illnesses such as HIV or TB where muscle wasting is common.

t.b: Assesses muscle strength; low values suggest functional loss despite hypertrophy.
Screening for muscle mass when imaging unavailable; <23 cm in adults may indicate wasting.
Quantifies hypertrophy; not always accessible, use MUAC as alternative.

b: Start with low‑load, high‑repetition exercises; increase load by 5‑10 % weekly.
Supplement with oral whey or soy protein if diet is deficient.
Treat HIV/TB with appropriate antimicrobials to reduce catabolism.
sections.p: Promote progressive resistance training, ensure protein intake of 1.2‑1.5 g/kg/day, and treat underlying catabolic conditions.

b: Hyperplasia is rare in humans; hypertrophy is the usual response to training.
Pseudohypertrophy shows weak strength despite larger girth.
sections.p: Muscle hyperplasia (increase in fiber number) and pseudohypertrophy (e.g., muscular dystrophy where fat replaces muscle).

b: Elevated CK often reflects muscle damage, not growth.
Body‑weight alone does not differentiate fat vs. muscle gain.
sections.p: Serum creatine kinase may be normal despite significant hypertrophy; rely on functional testing.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid, unexplained muscle swelling with pain, fever, or weakness (possible compartment syndrome).
Severe weakness despite apparent hypertrophy (may indicate myopathy).
